title: Individual productivity triples, but company delivery only goes from 20 days to 17
dek: AI armed everyone, but the organisation didn't get faster — because the weakest plank in the barrel isn't a person, it's the process. The real dividing line is whether you can rework the process and the organisation, not whether you hand out tokens to employees.
why: A frontline CEO explains the nuts and bolts of building his own CEO AI, cancelling the weekly meeting, and using token consumption to identify elite performers — the mechanisms and the numbers are concrete, and the decision-hub section in the back half is the most valuable part.
who: CEOs, CTOs and HR leads at companies currently pushing AI into practice, especially managers trying to work out why individuals got faster but the organisation didn't.
skip: The first 4 minutes of education-scenario setup can be fast-forwarded; go straight to the weakest-plank case at 16:07.

points.h: Individual productivity triples, delivery only gets three days faster
points.body: NetEase ran the numbers last year: a software requirement, from the product manager receiving it and producing a design doc to the feature going live, averaged 20 working days. After AI coding crossed the inflection point, many engineers doubled or even tripled-to-quintupled their personal efficiency, some tenfold. But for a feature of the same scope, the whole process only shrank from 20 days to 17. The reason is that a team completing a complex task is like a barrel: of the 20 planks, 10 are engineers, 3 are product, 3 are testing. The engineer and product-manager planks shoot up fast, but some planks aren't people at all — they're process, and they haven't improved one bit. So landing AI means clearing three hurdles: awareness, getting it into individuals' short-range tasks, and reworking process and organisation — the third is the hardest.

points.h: Cancel the weekly meeting: AI syncs information, humans only solve problems
points.body: Ruan Liang asked friends who run companies whether they still hold weekly meetings; 99% said yes. A weekly meeting usually serves three purposes: syncing information, spotting problems and opportunities, and making decisions. It used to run 2.5 hours a week, but the time spent on that meeting could be ten times 2.5 hours — every department prepares materials layer by layer, and the information sync itself isn't even done well, because nobody listens attentively the whole time and may miss the one sentence relevant to them. After the reform: the general manager and management agree on what information is needed, everyone fills in a template and stores it in the knowledge base, and AI scans and consolidates it into a focused, interactive HTML report you can leave comments and follow-up questions on; an AI agent produces a first pass of problems and opportunities, which human brains confirm and supplement; solving problems and making decisions move to dedicated meetings.

points.h: SaaS isn't dead, but ordinary SaaS will die
points.body: Ruan Liang doesn't think SaaS is dead: SaaS is essentially Service, and Service always exists, it just changes form — AI as a Service and Agent as a Service are themselves software. But ordinary SaaS may really die, while genuinely good SaaS that has already entered a company's critical processes will only get better, because it becomes internal infrastructure. In the past humans used software, limited by time and energy; in the future a mass of agents will call databases, APIs, security APIs, review APIs, HR APIs, CRM APIs — call volumes far exceeding the number and actions of humans, a massive increase, and the more it's called the more entrenched it becomes. The premise is that the Service itself is critical enough inside the company.

points.h: Distil your top salesperson into a skill and hand it to everyone
points.body: Two things give bosses headaches: the sales team has only one or two strong performers and the rest are mediocre; or a salesperson is so strong that if they leave, what then. There used to be no answer; now you can distil or extract a good salesperson's moves, scripts and behaviour into a skill. Two uses: distribute it to other salespeople to use directly; and have AI turn the elite salesperson into a teacher who trains ordinary salespeople. What training should distil isn't the salesperson, it's the customer — take the customer interaction data the salesperson has touched, calls, WeChat, email, and have AI simulate all kinds of customers to train salespeople. Online sales is fully digital and on record; for offline sales, recommend or even require a recording card — after a visit, while memory is fresh, record two or three minutes of voice notes, because salespeople dislike CRM (they think CRM is there to manage them) but don't mind a recording card, since it's also useful for their own customer review.

points.h: Fewer middle managers, strong individuals return to the front line with agent legions
points.body: Ruan Liang judges that middle management will shrink, though not necessarily by being eliminated — rather by going to the front line, and the front line can also carry a pile of agents. Middle managers performing management duties will become fewer and fewer, while elite people with formidable skills will become more and more numerous. He gives his engineering team as an example: socialised division of labour used to slice software development ever finer — frontend, backend, algorithm, test engineers; in the last half year it has visibly swung back to full-stack, everyone becoming a full-end engineer. The future organisation looks more and more like a distributed-peak structure: countless engineering peaks are very strong, one mother peak commands some of them, and countless agents fight a battle. He imagines a future interview negotiation: the candidate says I'm not one person, I bring an AI team, the summary of all my past experience and skills, and the premium the company has to pay might be some kind of OPC.

points.h: The AI value formula: quality times time saved
points.body: Ruan Liang offers a formula referencing a paper: AI's value = the quality with which AI completes the task (as a ratio of human quality) × time saved × the company's economic value per unit of time. For example, a human makes a cup of coffee at eight out of ten, AI also makes it at eight out of ten, so the quality coefficient is 1; a human takes 20 minutes, AI takes only 10 seconds, saving 14 minutes 50 seconds; multiply by the company's economic value per unit of time and you can compute the ROI. Prioritise four kinds of work for AI: things worth spending time on, high frequency, unavoidable, and where different people produce roughly the same result. Once computed, you can immediately decide whether to use AI for it. He also suggests first using the most expensive AI (Cloud, GPT) to prove the thing can be done, freeze the process, then switch to cheaper ones — if the most expensive can do it, within two months the cheap ones can too.

points.h: Crushing leads in token consumption, crushing leads in output too
points.body: NetEase started a points system in 2024, trying to quantify engineers' work into points with work value. By the AI era they found one kind of person whose token consumption is astonishing, and whose work output and work value are also astonishing, forming a statistical regularity: people with a crushing lead in token consumption are most likely building themselves a system, saving their own working time and increasing their thinking time, so their work quality and work results also lead by a crushing margin. Many bosses worry about waste from AI abuse; Ruan Liang's hot take is that genuinely excellent or elite people don't waste — the company has audits but doesn't tell colleagues, and through the statistics they found elite colleagues don't waste. He also says small companies embrace AI more thoroughly, because there are fewer organisational relationships, the boss uses it first, the hierarchy is shallow and the chain is short.

points.h: The core of a decision hub is decision history, not the model
points.body: Building an AI decision hub essentially requires a high-quality knowledge base, and what really matters is the historical decision processes and the basis for decisions. This year NetEase is preserving decisions that have happened historically and bringing them into the knowledge base; the two kinds of knowledge are combined to train an agent or skill, and then the original several hundred cases are fed back in for the agent to judge, with accuracy above 90%. Ruan Liang also mentions that Bridgewater gave researchers and analysts an agent it built itself, precipitating decision processes and decision history into a decision knowledge base; what Bridgewater does better is making the agent a learnable, evolvable part — after a person adjusts it, the confirmed adjustment enters the next round of reinforcement, keeping pace with the times, essentially human-machine collaborative self-evolution.

quotes.text: Across our whole process, for a software feature of similar scope, from the product requirement starting to going live, it only shrank from 20 days to 17.
The third and hardest hurdle to clear is actually reworking the process, your organisation — yes, once you rework the process, it inevitably means reworking the organisation.
In a two-and-a-half-hour meeting, it's impossible to be that focused every second — that would take a god.
Middle managers performing management duties will become fewer and fewer, but elite people with formidable skills should become more and more numerous.
If your token consumption leads by a crushing margin, your work quality and work results most likely lead by a crushing margin too.
Sometimes it's not that the boss wants to push and can push — because many organisations have ten thousand reasons to make sure the thing doesn't get done.
It made the agent into a learnable, evolvable part.
